title: Descriptive analysis
request: Home is where a problem becomes a solution: the user writes one sentence (or asks for any kind of model), brings data or not, and while the data is structured, cleaned and described in the background, a chat at the bottom asks a few questions about the real problem and an agent draws a solution workflow for this specific problem that follows the conversation. This package writes the small analysis the chat shows as the data becomes ready, and it must never relate a column to the outcome before the split.
spec: draft/analyze.py: size, kinds, missing values, distributions, top values, time coverage, feature-to-feature correlations and plain findings; nothing relates a column to the outcome. Done when the analysis tests pass, including the one that leaves the target and outcome-like columns out of the correlations.
plan: Write analyze(frame, target=None) returning plain JSON: a summary, the profile, per-column distributions, Spearman correlations between features only, and short findings.
Describe large tables from a seeded sample.
Leave the target and outcome-like columns out of the correlations.
Check the output survives json.dumps with allow_nan=False.

decisions.decision: Analysis before the split is descriptive only.
decisions.why: Any statistic linking a column to the outcome, computed on all rows, would inform choices with the future holdout's labels.

decisions.decision: Minute and hour time buckets are offered besides day to year.
Numbers are rounded to 4 decimals, or 4 significant digits below 1.
decisions.why: Large values stay readable and small rates do not round to zero.

change: dclab_rnd/draft/analyze.py with summary, profile, per-column distributions, feature-only correlations and highlights (many missing, duplicates, likely identifiers, near-constant columns, possible category codes, names suggesting a value known only after the outcome).

findings.defect: Narrow tables got no correlations at all.
findings.scenario: The first version left out every column the profile listed as a target candidate; the profile lists up to eight, so a table with about nine or fewer non-identifier columns had nothing left to correlate.
findings.cause: The exclusion rule used a broad candidate list where a narrow one was meant.
findings.fix: Correlations leave out the stated target and the columns whose names flag them as outcome-like, and nothing else.
findings.test: tests/test_draft_data.py: test_correlations_leave_out_the_target_and_outcome_like_columns, updated to the new rule.
findings.impact: On a table with about nine or fewer non-identifier columns, which covers many small business files, the chat's analysis showed no correlations at all. The user lost the one view of redundant features before choosing them, and the empty card looked like a finding.
findings.open: Outcome-like columns are found by their names. A column filled after the event under a neutral name is still correlated with the features and shown.

measurements.name: analysis speed
measurements.gate: Describing a large table must take about a second.
measurements.result: A 300,000-row CSV was analysed in 0.9 s from a seeded sample.
measurements.against_gate: The 300,000-row CSV was analysed in 0.9 s, which is about a second, as the gate asks.
limits: The time is for a seeded sample, not every row, so it says how fast the sample is described, not the full table.
The table was narrow and random; correlations among a few numeric columns cost little, and a wide table would cost more.
One run on one laptop, and 'about a second' was given no margin.

outcome: Done: the chat's analysis cards come from plain JSON; nothing relates a column to the outcome.
lessons: A leakage guard can be so broad that it removes the feature; say exactly which columns are excluded and why.
risks: Any statistic relating a column to the outcome, computed on all rows before the split, lets the holdout's labels inform choices (rule 1).
A guard that drops too many columns as outcome-like leaves nothing to describe on a narrow table.
A NaN or infinity in the output breaks the JSON the page reads.
Describing a very large table row by row is slow, and an unseeded sample gives a different description each time.
Rounding small rates to a fixed number of decimals shows a rare class as zero.
